analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax entirely.
analysis.headline: The estate tax repeal bill never got past a committee referral and died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the estate tax — the tax on wealth left behind at death — along with the gift tax and a related tax on transfers that skip a generation. The estate tax only applies to the largest estates, so its repeal would direct most of its benefit to the heirs of the wealthiest families, while the federal government would lose the revenue permanently. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates — generally families with more than the taxable threshold at death — would pay nothing on inherited wealth. Estate holders planning large lifetime gifts would also benefit from repeal of the gift tax. The bill's own findings argue family farms and small businesses would be spared liquidation to pay the tax.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax for all deaths and gifts after enactment, so no federal tax would apply to inherited wealth.

The bill's findings say repeal would boost savings and investment, help family businesses, and spare family farms from being sold to pay the tax, citing a claim that farmers are 15 times more likely than other Americans to face estate taxes.
Repeal applies to all decedents dying after enactment, not just below a threshold, so the largest estates get the full benefit immediately.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would permanently lose all estate, gift, and generation-skipping tax revenue. The bill includes no replacement revenue, so the cost would fall on taxpayers generally through larger deficits or cuts to other programs. Most of the tax's current burden falls on a small share of very large estates, so the tax relief would concentrate at the top.
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers via lost federal revenue

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the estate and gift taxes with no offsetting revenue, so the entire federal intake from these taxes — billions of dollars a year that fund general government programs — disappears permanently.
Because only the largest estates pay the estate tax, the benefit of repeal is concentrated among the wealthiest families rather than spread across ordinary taxpayers.

Repealing the gift tax alongside the estate tax would also let large lifetime wealth transfers go untaxed, removing the backstop that currently prevents people from avoiding income and transfer taxes by shifting wealth to family members.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a permanent, unconditional tax cut on inherited wealth with no revenue replacement. Its main fairness argument rests on family farms and small businesses, but because the tax applies only to the largest estates, the dollar value of repeal flows overwhelmingly to the biggest estates. An honest weighing: the emotional appeal to family farms is real, but the fiscal cost and the concentration of benefits make this a very top-heavy proposal as written.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Lugar introduced the Estate and Gift Tax Repeal Act of 1999 on January 19, 1999, joined by introductory cosponsors including Sens. Hagel, Roberts, and Helms.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action was ever taken: the Finance Committee never reported the bill, and it never received a floor vote in either chamber before the 106th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury kept estate, gift, and generation-skipping tax revenue, and the general taxpayers who fund government programs were spared the cost of an unreplaced tax cut. The wealthiest estates, which pay most of the estate tax, would have been the direct winners had it passed — instead they remain subject to the tax.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers; the wealthiest estates lost out

for.name: Sen. Richard G. Lugar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the estate and gift tax repeal bill and delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: 5 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrats signed on.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill.

industries.industry: Wealthiest households (largest estates and their heirs)
industries.note: Because the estate tax applies only to the largest estates, these families would have been the primary beneficiaries of repeal; the bill's failure means their estates remain taxable. Repeal with no revenue replacement would have shifted the cost to general taxpayers.

industries.industry: Estate planning attorneys and trust services
industries.note: This industry's revenue depends on the existence of the estate and gift taxes, since families pay for planning to reduce or avoid them; repeal would have eliminated much of that market. Its interest runs against repeal, which in this case aligned with preserving the tax on very large estates.
Life insurance used to cover expected estate tax bills is a large market that repeal would have shrunk. As with estate planners, the industry benefits from the tax remaining on the books.

The bill's findings argue farmers are disproportionately exposed to the estate tax and repeal would spare heirs from selling land or businesses to pay it. If true, this is the one group of working owners with a direct stake in repeal.
